transcript.content: Hello, please have a seat. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, thank you. Yeah, I'll just sit right here. So, um, what brings me in... well, it’s mostly work stuff. I work at a meat processing plant right now. I actually just got my bachelor's degree not that long ago, but you know how the job market is, so I took this job at the processing facility. It’s hard work, but it’s fine. The thing is, though, the regulations there are incredibly strict, which makes total sense, obviously, with food safety and everything being so heavily monitored. 

But the main issue I'm having, and the reason I made this appointment, is that I keep starting things—like the sanitation steps for the processing equipment, or the batch logs for the different cuts of meat, or even just the basic end-of-line paperwork—and I somehow always manage to leave out the last parts. I'll get all set up, I'll be doing the first few steps perfectly, filling out the top half of the form or doing the initial chemical spray-down, and then I just... don't finish it. 

And it's driving me absolutely crazy because it’s not like I don't care! I know my job completely depends on finishing them correctly. If I don't sign off on that very last box on the batch log or finish the final rinse step in the sanitation protocol, it's a huge compliance issue for the whole plant. My supervisor gets so mad, and I get so mad at myself, because I know the steps. I have a degree, I should be able to just complete a simple daily checklist, but I just drop the ball at the very end almost every single time. I'll think I'm done, or I'll just somehow walk away from it, and I don't know why I can't just push through to the actual end of the task...
Did you experience similar difficulties with finishing tasks or staying focused while growing up in school?

Oh, absolutely. Yeah, it's actually funny you ask that—well, not funny haha, but... my mom actually still has all my old elementary school report cards. She keeps them in this big plastic bin at her house, and the ones from around fourth grade are just... they're honestly kind of depressing to read now. Every single teacher wrote the exact same thing. They'd always say that I was a really bright kid, that I had all this potential, but that I needed constant—and I mean *constant*—reminders to just finish my classwork or to actually turn in my homework. I'd do the homework, or at least start it, and then it would just vanish into the black hole of my backpack and never make it to the teacher's desk. 

And the thing is, I remember actually understanding the lessons. The material itself wasn't too hard for me at all, I understood the concepts they were teaching perfectly fine, but when they would give out the instructions for what we were supposed to do with that information, I would just completely miss huge chunks of what they were saying. It was like I was sitting right there, looking at them, but my brain was just somewhere else entirely. The only way I ever actually got all the steps down was if the teacher physically came over and stayed close to my desk to make sure I was tracking. 

And it just makes me so upset thinking about it now, because it’s the exact same thing happening at the plant, you know? Just... doing all the work to understand the job, getting halfway through, and then failing at the very last step of actually turning the paper in or finishing the task. It’s like nothing has changed since I was nine years old. I have a whole bachelor's degree now, and I'm still that same kid who can't just finish a simple worksheet without someone standing over my shoulder. It's just exhausting.
Do you often feel restless, fidgety, or have trouble sitting still?

No, not really. Honestly, it’s kind of the exact opposite for me. I don't really have that physical restlessness at all. Like, I can sit completely still for hours. When I was getting my bachelor's degree, I would sit in these massive, three-hour lecture halls and not move a single muscle. I had a roommate who used to bounce her leg constantly when we studied, like just shaking the whole table, and I never did anything like that. But the thing is, even though my body was perfectly still, it’s like my brain was just... gone. Just completely checked out and floating out the window. 

Even now at the processing plant, we have these mandatory safety briefings in the breakroom sometimes—and they are *so* long, they literally bring in these giant binders and just read off the updated OSHA guidelines and chemical handling protocols for what feels like an absolute eternity—and I’m perfectly fine just sitting there in those terrible hard plastic chairs. I’m not tapping my feet, I’m not playing with my pen, I don't feel like I need to jump out of my skin or pace around the room or anything like that. 

People probably look at me during those meetings and think I’m the most attentive person in the room because I’m just staring straight ahead, completely motionless. But in reality, I haven't heard a single word the safety manager said for the last twenty minutes. So yeah, the physical sitting still part? I'm totally fine with that. I don't get that restless feeling in my body at all. I just sit there like a statue, but my mind is just a million miles away, you know?
